title: Closure-channel identifiability and two-channel recovery in monatomic kinetic normal shocks
summary: Residual agreement in a kinetic or moment equation does not automatically identify every higher-order closure variable entering a nonequilibrium shock. We formulate this issue as an observability problem for the fourth-order closure content of monatomic normal shocks and follow it through a hierarchy of collision models and diagnostics. The kinematic part of the result is independent of the collision operator: the one-dimensional heat-flux budget observes the projected fourth-order channel $S=R^{\cl}_{xx}+Δ/3$, not the tensorial R26-level moment $R^{\cl}_{xx}$ separately from the scalar fourth-order excess $Δ$. The observation map therefore has a one-dimensional null space, so a heat-flux residual can be small while the split between tensorial anisotropy and isotropic tail intensity remains wrong. A DVM-consistent scalar-excess budget supplies the missing channel and gives the two-channel reconstruction $R^{\cl}_{xx}=S-Δ/3$ without direct $R^{\cl}_{xx}$ data. Across BGK shocks at Mach 2--5, this reduces the active-zone $R^{\cl}_{xx}$ error from about $63$--$64\%$ to $2.4$--$4.1\%$. Sparse scalar-excess interpolation is used only as an information-reduction test: a representative 24-probe operating point gives $R^{\cl}_{xx}$ errors below $4.5\%$, and below $4.7\%$ with $1\%$ probe noise. Collision-model diagnostics then separate the invariant observation channel from the model-dependent source law. Shakhov changes the heat-flux relaxation to the correct Prandtl number but is neutral in the even $|\boldsymbol c|^4$ scalar-excess source; a direct discrete Shakhov channel check recovers $S$, $Δ$ and $R^{\cl}_{xx}$ with errors $6.4\times10^{-4}$, $2.1\times10^{-7}$ and $1.0\times10^{-3}$, respectively.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies an observability problem in kinetic/moment equations where residual agreement does not guarantee correct identification of higher-order closure variables in nonequilibrium shocks. The authors show that the one-dimensional heat-flux budget observes a projected fourth-order channel S = R^cl_xx + Δ/3, not the separate R26-level moment R^cl_xx and scalar fourth-order excess Δ. By adding a DVM-consistent scalar-excess budget, two-channel reconstruction reduces active-zone R^cl_xx errors from ~63-64% to 2.4-4.1% across BGK shocks at Mach 2-5. Sparse interpolation with 24 probes yields errors below 4.5%, and below 4.7% with 1% noise. Shakhov collision model changes heat-flux relaxation but is neutral in the scalar-excess source, with direct channel check recovering S, Δ, and R^cl_xx with errors 6.4×10⁻⁴, 2.1×10⁻⁷, and 1.0×10⁻³ respectively.
AI.motivation: To address the observability problem where residual agreement in kinetic/moment equations fails to uniquely identify higher-order closure variables (specifically the fourth-order channel) in nonequilibrium shocks, which leads to hidden errors in tensorial anisotropy versus isotropic tail intensity even when heat-flux residuals appear small.
AI.method: Formulates the issue as an observability problem for fourth-order closure content in monatomic normal shocks through a hierarchy of collision models and diagnostics. Uses DVM-consistent scalar-excess budget to provide the missing observation channel and reconstructs R^cl_xx via two-channel reconstruction. Tests across BGK shocks at Mach 2-5 with sparse scalar-excess interpolation and collision-model diagnostics using Shakhov model.
AI.result: The one-dimensional heat-flux budget observes S = R^cl_xx + Δ/3, not R^cl_xx and Δ separately; a one-dimensional null space exists in the observation map. Adding scalar-excess budget reduces active-zone R^cl_xx error from ~63-64% to 2.4-4.1%. Sparse 24-probe interpolation gives errors below 4.5% (below 4.7% with 1% noise). Shakhov direct channel check recovers S, Δ, and R^cl_xx with errors 6.4×10⁻⁴, 2.1×10⁻⁷, and 1.0×10⁻³.
AI.conclusion: The kinematic part of the observation problem is independent of the collision operator; the heat-flux residual alone is insufficient to identify the split between tensorial anisotropy and isotropic tail intensity. Using a scalar-excess budget resolves the ambiguity and dramatically reduces reconstruction errors. Collision-model diagnostics separate the invariant observation channel from model-dependent source law, with Shakhov being neutral in the even fourth-order scalar-excess source.

title: Black Hole Polarimetry III: Universal Polarization of Synchrotron Radiation at the Horizon
summary: Polarized images of a black hole encode the direction of electromagnetic energy flow near its event horizon. Measuring polarization from near-horizon emission can determine whether this energy flow is powered by the accreting plasma or the black hole spin. Here we consider the linear polarization of synchrotron radiation emitted from the base of horizon-threading field lines in a time-stationary, axisymmetric, and degenerate Kerr magnetosphere. We show that the observed polarization pattern displays universal behavior: it is completely determined by the black hole spin and observer inclination and is independent of the magnetic field geometry. We derive a simple analytic formula for this spin-dependent horizon polarization pattern. We find that this predicted pattern is also approached in time-averaged images from General Relativistic Magnetohydrodynamic simulations. Future observations with Very-Long-Baseline Interferometry at microarcsecond resolution could detect the trend of polarization toward the unique horizon value in M87*. Such observations may enable new measurements of black hole spin and provide evidence that magnetic field lines thread the horizon and extract spin energy via the Blandford--Znajek process.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that linear polarization of synchrotron radiation from the base of horizon-threading field lines in a Kerr magnetosphere exhibits a universal pattern determined solely by black hole spin and observer inclination, independent of magnetic field geometry, with implications for measuring black hole spin and detecting the Blandford-Znajek process in M87*.
AI.motivation: To determine whether near-horizon electromagnetic energy flow is powered by accreting plasma or black hole spin, by measuring polarization from emission near the event horizon.
AI.method: Analytical derivation of linear polarization from synchrotron radiation at the base of horizon-threading field lines in a time-stationary, axisymmetric, degenerate Kerr magnetosphere, validated against time-averaged GRMHD simulations.
AI.result: The observed polarization pattern is universal — determined only by black hole spin and observer inclination, independent of magnetic field geometry — and can be expressed via a simple analytic formula. This pattern is also approached in time-averaged GRMHD simulations.
AI.conclusion: Future VLBI observations at microarcsecond resolution could detect this horizon polarization trend in M87*, enabling new measurements of black hole spin and providing evidence for magnetic field lines threading the horizon and extracting spin energy via the Blandford-Znajek process.

title: Implementation of multi-grid Poisson solver in numerical relativity and its application to gravitational collapse of massive star
summary: We develop a new grid-based multi-grid Poisson solver in numerical relativity. We report the performance of the multi-grid Poisson solver in the initial value problems for two-puncture black holes, a static spherical neutron star, a uniformly rotating neutron star in equilibrium, and a gravitationally collapsing massive star. As a demonstration, we conduct a numerical-relativity neutrino-radiation-transfer hydrodynamics simulation of the gravitational collapse of the $9M_\odot$ massive star in Ref.~\cite{Aguilera-Dena:2020mfh} up to the core bounce. During the simulation, we employ the constraint-preserving regird prescription with the newly developed multi-grid Poisson solver to improve the resolution. It shows that the baryonic mass, the Arnowit-Deser-Misner (ADM) mass, and the ADM-like angular momentum are, respectively, preserved with $O(10^{-3})\%$ and $O(10^{-2})$--$O(10^{-1})$\% accuracy.

AI.tldr: A new grid-based multi-grid Poisson solver for numerical relativity is developed and tested on various astrophysical scenarios (binary black holes, neutron stars, collapsing massive star). It demonstrates high conservation accuracy for baryonic mass, ADM mass, and angular momentum in a core-collapse supernova simulation.
AI.motivation: To develop a more accurate and efficient Poisson solver for constraint equations in numerical relativity, particularly needed for simulations involving diverse astrophysical objects with improved resolution handling.
AI.method: A grid-based multi-grid Poisson solver is developed and integrated with a constraint-preserving regrid prescription. It is tested on two-puncture black holes, static/rotating neutron stars, and a gravitationally collapsing 9 M⊙ massive star, with a full neutrino-radiation-transfer hydrodynamics simulation up to core bounce.
AI.result: Baryonic mass, ADM mass, and ADM-like angular momentum are preserved with O(10⁻³)% and O(10⁻²)–O(10⁻¹)% accuracy, respectively.
AI.conclusion: The multi-grid Poisson solver is effective for constraint-preserving regridding in numerical relativity, achieving high conservation accuracy across diverse astrophysical simulations.

title: Spectral analysis of magnetized advective accretion flows around rotating black holes
comment: 20 pages including 16 figures (32 png files) and 2 tables; accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: The spectra of an accretion disk around black holes are the basic diagnostic tool to enlighten the underlying flows and then black holes. Accretion flows around black holes, however, are controlled by parameters like the magnetic field, spin of the black hole, accretion rate and temperature of the flow. These quantities affect the (magneto)hydrodynamics of the flow thus consequently lead to variations in the spectrum. We first consider numerical steady state magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) solutions of magnetized accretion flows around black holes to study the dependence of the spectra on these disk properties. The spectrum exhibits strong dependence on the spin of the black hole, accretion rate, magnetic field and the electron temperature of the flow. Variations in these quantities influence the emission peaks and overall luminosity, which can be a tell-tale sign to extract physics of observed spectra. We further validate our results with general relativistic MHD (GRMHD) simulations using the standard and normal evolution (SANE) and magnetically arrested disk (MAD) vector potentials. We consider two black hole spins ($a=0.5$ and $a=0.9375$) to model the magnetic field configurations and study the resulting spectra by comparing MAD and SANE results. We find a large difference in the bolometric luminosities and the location of the emission peaks between SANE and MAD flows. Certain properties of the spectra, like, the ratio of synchrotron radiation to synchrotron self-Comptonization peaks in SANE and MAD, show drastically distinct features. The overall luminosity combined with such metrics can distinguish the magnetic field characteristics in astrophysical systems.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how black hole accretion disk spectra depend on parameters like black hole spin, accretion rate, magnetic field, and electron temperature, using both steady-state MHD solutions and GRMHD simulations (SANE vs. MAD configurations). The spectra show strong sensitivity to these parameters, with distinct features in bolometric luminosity and emission peak locations between SANE and MAD flows, enabling the extraction of magnetic field properties from observed spectra.
AI.motivation: To understand how key physical parameters (magnetic field, black hole spin, accretion rate, electron temperature) influence the spectra of accretion flows around black holes, and to identify spectral signatures that can reveal the underlying physics of observed systems.
AI.method: The authors first compute numerical steady-state MHD solutions for magnetized accretion flows. They then validate these results using GRMHD simulations with SANE and MAD magnetic field configurations, considering black hole spins of a=0.5 and a=0.9375, and compare the resulting spectra.
AI.result: The spectrum strongly depends on black hole spin, accretion rate, magnetic field, and electron temperature. Large differences are found in bolometric luminosities and emission peak locations between SANE and MAD flows. The ratio of synchrotron to synchrotron self-Comptonization peaks shows drastically distinct features between the two configurations.
AI.conclusion: The overall luminosity combined with spectral metrics like the synchrotron-to-SSC peak ratio can distinguish magnetic field characteristics in astrophysical systems, providing a diagnostic tool to infer the magnetic field configuration around black holes from observed spectra.

title: TBD LBD: The nature of `little blue dots'
comment: 5 pages, 5 figures, submitted. Comments are welcome
summary: Previous Sirocco radiative-transfer models of gas-cocooned AGN predicted lower-column counterparts to little red dots (LRDs): compact, X-ray-weak sources with bluer continuum slopes and Balmer jumps rather than Balmer breaks. The recently identified population of little blue dots (LBDs) closely resembles this predicted phase. Here we explore these lower-column-density cocoons in which nebular recombination emission remains visible while strong Balmer-continuum absorption is avoided. We find that a sequence of increasing column density connects more classical AGN spectra, Balmer-jump LBD-like spectra at $N_{\rm H}\!\sim\!{\rm few}\times10^{24} \mathrm{cm^{-2}}$, and Balmer-break LRD-like spectra at higher columns. In this sequence, electron scattering produces exponential line wings and suppresses X-ray emission before strong Balmer absorption features, characteristic of higher column densities, appear. We therefore propose that LBDs are lower-column analogues of LRDs within a common gas-cocooned AGN sequence. This interpretation predicts that Balmer-jump emission, X-ray weakness, permitted lines with exponential wings, He II $λ$4686 emission, smaller H$α$ FWHM values and equivalent widths than in LRDs, and weak or absent absorption features are characteristic of LBDs. We compare to three example LBD spectra and identify Balmer-jump signatures in them.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that Little Blue Dots (LBDs) are lower-column-density analogues of Little Red Dots (LRDs) within a common gas-cocooned AGN sequence, where increasing column density transitions from classical AGN spectra through Balmer-jump LBDs to Balmer-break LRDs.
AI.motivation: To explain the recently identified population of Little Blue Dots (LBDs) as a predicted lower-column-density phase of gas-cocooned AGN, bridging classical AGN and Little Red Dots (LRDs).
AI.method: Radiative-transfer modeling of gas-cocooned AGN across a sequence of increasing column density, comparing predicted spectral features to observed LBD spectra.
AI.result: LBDs exhibit Balmer jumps (not breaks), X-ray weakness, exponential line wings, He II λ4686 emission, smaller Hα FWHM and EWs than LRDs, and weak/absent absorption features, consistent with NH ~ few×10²³ cm⁻².
AI.conclusion: LBDs are lower-column analogues of LRDs within a unified gas-cocooned AGN sequence, with electron scattering suppressing X-rays before strong Balmer absorption appears.

title: Spectroscopic modeling of ionic structure in stellar winds of high-mass X-ray binaries
summary: High-mass X-ray binaries (HMXBs) provide a natural laboratory to study radiatively driven stellar winds under strong external X-ray irradiation. As the compact object moves along its orbit, the wind density and ionization structure vary with orbital phase, leaving characteristic signatures in X-ray emission and absorption features. The amplitude and morphology of this variability depend on the system geometry, including the orbital inclination (via line-of-sight and occultation effects) and the orbital eccentricity (via phase-dependent changes in the orbital separation). We present a computational framework that connects phase-resolved spectroscopic variability to the three-dimensional structure of irradiated winds, and that enables inference of physically meaningful wind--irradiation parameters within a Bayesian setting. We combine photoionization calculations with a parametric wind description and orbital geometry to construct three-dimensional maps of density and ionization. From these maps we compute orbital-phase-dependent diagnostics, accounting for geometric occultation and wind inhomogeneity through a clumping prescription. We then use Bayesian inference to compare model predictions with phase-resolved observables and to quantify parameter constraints and degeneracies. The framework reproduces the main orbital-phase-dependent trends expected for irradiated winds and yields robust constraints on the system ionization balance. While combinations of wind and luminosity parameters are well constrained, individual parameters can remain partially degenerate depending on the orbital configuration and data quality. This modular and computationally efficient approach provides a route to interpret HMXB phase variability in physical terms, and offers a foundation for future extensions toward forward spectral modeling and population-level applications.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a computational framework that combines photoionization calculations, parametric wind models, and orbital geometry to generate 3D maps of irradiated stellar winds in HMXBs, enabling Bayesian inference of wind-irradiation parameters from phase-resolved spectroscopic data.
AI.motivation: HMXBs serve as natural laboratories for studying how external X-ray irradiation affects radiatively driven stellar winds, but the relationship between phase-resolved spectroscopic variability and underlying wind/ionization structure is complex and not well constrained.
AI.method: The framework integrates photoionization calculations with a parametric wind description and orbital geometry to build 3D density and ionization maps, then computes phase-dependent diagnostics accounting for occultation and clumping. Bayesian inference is used to compare model predictions with observables.
AI.result: The framework reproduces expected orbital-phase-dependent trends for irradiated winds, yields robust constraints on system ionization balance, and shows that combinations of wind and luminosity parameters are well constrained, though individual parameters can be partially degenerate depending on orbital configuration and data quality.
AI.conclusion: This modular and computationally efficient approach provides a physically grounded method to interpret HMXB phase variability, with potential for extension toward forward spectral modeling and population-level studies.

title: Unification models of Active Galactic Nuclei
comment: Invited chapter for the Encyclopedia of Astrophysics (edited by I. Mandel, section editor S. McGee) to be published by Elsevier as a Reference Module
summary: This chapter presents an overview of the unification models for Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN), focusing on the physical structures, classification schemes, and evolutionary processes that characterize accreting supermassive black holes. We introduce the fundamental components of AGN, including the supermassive black hole, accretion disk, jets, outflows, broad-line and narrow-line regions, polar dust and the dusty anisotropic obscurer. The traditional orientation-based unification model is reviewed, with a focus on the role of the covering factor of the obscuring material in shaping observed properties. We introduce the radiation-regulated unification model, which accounts for the influence of radiative feedback on the nuclear environment of SMBHs. We also examine the evolutionary aspects of AGN unification, including the impact of galaxy mergers, host galaxy properties, and redshift-dependent trends. Finally, we discuss changing-look AGN, which challenge conventional unification frameworks by exhibiting dramatic spectral variability.

AI.tldr: This chapter provides an overview of AGN unification models, covering physical structures, classification schemes, and evolutionary processes of accreting supermassive black holes, including traditional orientation-based unification, radiation-regulated unification, evolutionary trends, and changing-look AGN.
AI.motivation: To synthesize current understanding of AGN unification by reviewing physical components, classification schemes, and evolutionary processes to address the diversity of observed AGN properties.
AI.method: Review of traditional orientation-based unification model (focusing on obscuring material covering factor) and radiation-regulated unification model (accounting for radiative feedback effects), alongside analysis of evolutionary aspects such as galaxy mergers, host galaxy properties, and redshift-dependent trends.
AI.result: Identification that covering factor of obscuring material is key in orientation-based unification; radiative feedback significantly influences the nuclear environment; galaxy mergers and host properties drive evolutionary unification; changing-look AGN challenge conventional frameworks through dramatic spectral variability.
AI.conclusion: AGN unification requires integrating orientation effects, radiation feedback, and evolutionary processes, while changing-look AGN suggest the need for dynamical unification models beyond static geometric frameworks.

title: Data-driven modeling of Galactic diffuse emission with multi-wavelength observations
summary: We present a data-driven investigation of Galactic diffuse emission. Using multi-frequency Planck radio/microwave maps (30-857 GHz) and Fermi-LAT gamma-ray data (50 MeV-814 GeV), we construct a nonlinear mapping between radio emission and gamma-ray intensity through supervised machine learning. Our models achieve high predictive accuracy (R^2 > 0.90 in the 0.1-10 GeV range), demonstrating that multi-frequency radio observations encode sufficient information to reconstruct both spatial morphology and spectral properties of diffuse gamma-ray emission. By analyzing model performance across different frequency bands and spatial regions, we identify high-frequency radio bands as the dominant predictor, providing direct empirical support for the hadronic origin of Galactic 0.1-10 GeV gamma rays, while low-frequency radio bands for the leptonic origin above 10 GeV. Residual maps reveal coherent large-scale structures, including Loop I and III, highlighting regions where standard interstellar emission models are incomplete or biased. Compared with the GALPROP model, our machine learning approach yields a higher R^2=0.95 and lower mean absolute relative error (14.7%) in the inner Galactic disk and the Galactic center region. Our results illustrate that machine learning serves as a physically interpretable tool for multi-messenger astrophysics, providing a data-driven baseline for separating non-standard emission components and deriving new constraints on cosmic-ray propagation and interstellar medium structure.

AI.tldr: The paper uses supervised machine learning to map multi-frequency Planck radio data (30-857 GHz) to Fermi-LAT gamma-ray emission (50 MeV-814 GeV), achieving high predictive accuracy (R²>0.90 at 0.1-10 GeV). High-frequency radio bands dominate predictions for 0.1-10 GeV gamma rays (supporting hadronic origin), while low-frequency bands dominate above 10 GeV (leptonic origin). Residuals reveal Loop I and III structures missed by standard models. The ML approach outperforms GALPROP (R²=0.95 vs lower, MARE=14.7%) in the inner Galactic disk and center.
AI.motivation: To investigate Galactic diffuse emission by constructing a nonlinear data-driven mapping between multi-frequency radio and gamma-ray observations, overcoming limitations of traditional physical models like GALPROP and identifying missing emission components.
AI.method: Supervised machine learning using multi-frequency Planck maps (30-857 GHz) as input features and Fermi-LAT gamma-ray data (50 MeV-814 GeV) as targets, trained to predict gamma-ray intensity nonlinearly from radio data.
AI.result: Achieved R²>0.90 in the 0.1-10 GeV range. High-frequency radio bands are dominant predictors for 0.1-10 GeV gamma rays (hadronic origin), low-frequency bands for >10 GeV (leptonic origin). Residual maps reveal Loop I and III. Outperforms GALPROP with R²=0.95 and MARE=14.7% in the inner Galactic disk and center.
AI.conclusion: Machine learning provides a physically interpretable, data-driven tool for multi-messenger astrophysics, offering a baseline to separate non-standard emission components and derive new constraints on cosmic-ray propagation and ISM structure.

title: Bar-induced migration of $ω$ Centauri away from Gaia Sausage-Enceladus
summary: The globular cluster $ω$ Cen has been suggested to have originated in the Gaia Sausage-Enceladus (GSE) merger event, possibly as its nuclear star cluster. However, the present-day orbits of $ω$ Cen and the GSE debris are very different. We investigate the scenario in which $ω$ Cen originated in the GSE and migrated to its current position due to perturbations from the Galactic bar. The [$α$/M] distributions of stars located between the GSE debris and $ω$ Cen in $(L_z,E)$ space tentatively support this scenario, but are not conclusive. We run simulations of the GSE debris and $ω$ Cen in a realistic Milky Way potential with a decelerating bar at various present-day pattern speeds. We find that $ω$ Cen can indeed be traced back to the phase space region occupied by the GSE debris. However, this likely requires a pattern speed of $Ω_\mathrm{b}\lesssim26$ km s$^{-1}$ kpc$^{-1}$, which is much lower than most recent estimates. We conclude that a GSE origin for $ω$ Cen is dynamically and chemically plausible, but this would require a re-evaluation of the current consensus on the bar's pattern speed.

AI.tldr: The paper explores whether ω Cen (a globular cluster) could have originated from the Gaia Sausage-Enceladus (GSE) merger and migrated to its current orbit due to Galactic bar perturbations. Simulations suggest this is dynamically and chemically plausible but require a bar pattern speed ≤26 km/s/kpc, lower than current estimates.
AI.motivation: To reconcile the conflicting orbital evidence for ω Cen's proposed origin in the GSE merger event, by investigating bar-driven migration as a possible mechanism.
AI.method: Chemical analysis of [α/M] distributions in (L_z, E) space between GSE debris and ω Cen, combined with N-body simulations of GSE debris and ω Cen in a realistic Milky Way potential with a decelerating Galactic bar at various pattern speeds.
AI.result: ω Cen can be dynamically traced back to the GSE phase-space region, but this likely requires a bar pattern speed Ω_b ≲ 26 km/s/kpc, significantly lower than most recent observational estimates.
AI.conclusion: A GSE origin for ω Cen is dynamically and chemically plausible, but it would necessitate revising the currently accepted bar pattern speed to a lower value.

title: Constraining inhomogeneities and asymmetries in SNe, FBOTs, and other high-energy transients from unresolved radio observations
summary: Synchrotron emission in high-energy transients is produced by relativistic electrons accelerated by shocks. As high-energy transients are often unresolved even on angular scales probed by very long baseline interferometry, it is difficult to obtain a full picture of the ejecta and circumstellar medium (CSM) properties that are probed by the radio synchrotron emission. Radio spectra of high-energy transients frequently show optically thick slopes shallower than the standard $F_ν\propto ν^{5/2}$ expected from synchrotron self-absorption (SSA) models, or broader spectra near the self-absorption frequency. Such deviations are often interpreted phenomenologically, without providing clear insights into the structure of the emitting region. We show how information on the homogeneity and symmetry of the emitting region can be directly inferred from SSA spectra, even when the source is unresolved. We discuss the circumstances under which inhomogeneities in the emitting region can change the spectrum below the self-absorption frequency, causing it to follow a different slope. We examine which parameters can be constrained from observations and which remain degenerate. We apply this method to the stripped-envelope supernova (SN) 2016coi and to the fast blue optical transient (FBOT) AT2018cow, showing that SSA spectra constrain the degree of inhomogeneity in these systems, providing strong evidence for inhomogeneities in the emitting region in the SN 2016coi, and asymmetry in the case of AT2018cow, and we infer the characteristics of the emitting region. When well sampled spectra are available, our method can be applied as a general, model-independent, inference method. This approach can be used to constrain inhomogeneities in a variety of unresolved high-energy astrophysical transients, including SNe, FBOTs, tidal disruption events and gamma-ray bursts.

AI.tldr: The paper shows how synchrotron self-absorption (SSA) spectra can reveal inhomogeneities and asymmetries in unresolved high-energy transients, applying the method to SN 2016coi (finding inhomogeneous emission) and AT2018cow (finding asymmetry).
AI.motivation: Radio spectra of high-energy transients often show optically thick slopes shallower than the standard $F_ν \propto ν^{5/2}$ predicted by homogeneous SSA models, yet such deviations are typically treated phenomenologically without linking them to the physical structure of the emitting region.
AI.method: The authors derive how inhomogeneities and asymmetries in the emitting region modify the SSA spectrum below the self-absorption frequency, and develop a model-independent inference method to constrain these properties from unresolved radio spectra.
AI.result: Application to SN 2016coi provides strong evidence for inhomogeneities in the emitting region, while AT2018cow shows evidence for asymmetry. The method constrains the degree of inhomogeneity and characteristics of the emitting region from well-sampled spectra.
AI.conclusion: SSA spectra can directly inform on the homogeneity and symmetry of emitting regions even in unresolved sources, offering a general, model-independent tool applicable to various high-energy transients (SNe, FBOTs, TDEs, GRBs).

title: The Hubble Missing Globular Clusters Survey IV. Ultra-faint compact satellites of the Milky Way. The case of Koposov 2
comment: 16 pages, 13 figures, submitted to A&A. Comments are welcome
summary: In the last decades a number of extremely faint and compact Galactic satellites (Ultra Faint Compact Satellites; UFCS) have been discovered by large panoramic surveys. Their nature is uncertain due to their location in the overlapping dwarf galaxy-star cluster region of the $M_V-R_h$ plane and their faintness and distance. Here we show how the deep HST photometry from the Missing Globular Clusters Survey (MGCS), combined with spectroscopic metallicities, provides new insight into the nature of these satellites through accurate distance and age estimates. We consider the case of Koposov 2, currently the most metal-poor bound star cluster known in the entire Milky Way or an extreme case of Ultra Faint Dwarf galaxy. By performing a spectroscopically-informed bayesian isochrone fit on the MGCS data we find $(m-M)_0=16.85\pm 0.06$ ($D=23.4\pm 0.6$ kpc) and age=$13.7^{+0.9}_{-1.3}$ Gyr, showing that, contrary to previous age estimates, Koposov 2 is as old as the oldest Galactic globular clusters. The luminosity function, corrected for incompleteness, is well reproduced by a model with the same age and metallicity and a slope of the mass function $x=-0.35$, suggesting a significant depletion of faint stars. We model the surface stellar density field, deriving new robust estimates of the half-light radius ($R_h=0.39^{+0.06}_{-0.04}$ arcsec, corresponding to $R_h=2.7^{+0.4}_{-0.3}$ pc), of the absolute integrated magnitude ($M_V=-0.95\pm0.22$) and of the stellar mass ($M_{\star}=371.8\pm41.6M_{\odot}$), showing that Koposov 2 is much more compact than dwarf galaxies of similar stellar mass. The new evidence significantly support the hypothesis that Koposov 2 is a star cluster that may have lost a large fraction of its original mass. Finally we show that most UFCS lie in the same locus of the $M_V - R_h$ plane as Galactic open clusters, hinting to a possible additional channel for their formation.

AI.tldr: Using deep HST photometry and spectroscopic metallicities, this paper reclassifies Koposov 2 as an old, metal-poor globular cluster (age ~13.7 Gyr, D~23.4 kpc) that has lost significant mass, rather than an ultra-faint dwarf galaxy, and suggests most Ultra Faint Compact Satellites occupy the same locus as Galactic open clusters in the M_V-R_h plane.
AI.motivation: The nature of Ultra Faint Compact Satellites (UFCS) is uncertain because they lie in the overlapping region between dwarf galaxies and star clusters on the M_V-R_h plane, and their faintness and distance make classification difficult.
AI.method: Spectroscopically-informed Bayesian isochrone fitting on deep HST photometry from the Missing Globular Clusters Survey (MGCS), combined with luminosity function modeling and surface stellar density field analysis.
AI.result: Koposov 2 is as old as the oldest Galactic globular clusters (13.7^{+0.9}_{-1.3} Gyr) at D=23.4±0.6 kpc, with a half-light radius of 2.7^{+0.4}_{-0.3} pc, M_V=-0.95±0.22, stellar mass 371.8±41.6 M⊙, and a mass function slope x=-0.35 indicating significant depletion of faint stars. Most UFCS lie in the same locus as Galactic open clusters.
AI.conclusion: Koposov 2 is likely a star cluster that has lost a large fraction of its original mass, not an ultra-faint dwarf galaxy. The locus of UFCS overlapping with open clusters suggests an additional formation channel for these satellites.

title: Gravitational wave background from extreme-mass-ratio inspirals
summary: The gravitational wave background (GWB) produced by extreme-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs) serves as a powerful tool for probing the astrophysical and dynamical processes in galactic centers. EMRI systems are a primary target for the space-based detector LISA due to their long-lived signals and high signal-to-noise ratios. This study explores the statistical properties of the GWB from EMRI, focusing on the calculation methods for the GWB, the astrophysical distribution of EMRI sources, and the influence of key parameters, including the spin of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) and the masses of compact objects (COs). By analyzing these factors, we determine the distribution range of the characteristic strain of the GWB from EMRIs. We find that the final eccentricity distributions appear to have negligible effect on the intensity of the GWB due to rapid circularization before they become detectable and the spin of the SMBH enhances the GW characteristic strain by approximately 1$\%$ compared to cases without spin effects. The masses of COs can also significantly affect the characteristic strain of the GWB from EMRIs, with Black Hole (BH) as CO producing a GW signal intensity that is approximately one order of magnitude higher compared to cases where Neutron Star (NS) or White Dwarf (WD) are the COs.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the gravitational wave background (GWB) from extreme-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs), focusing on calculation methods, astrophysical source distributions, and the impact of SMBH spin and compact object masses. It finds that eccentricity has negligible effect due to rapid circularization, SMBH spin enhances GWB strain by ~1%, and BH compact objects produce ~10× stronger signals than NS or WD counterparts.
AI.motivation: EMRIs are primary targets for LISA; understanding their GWB enables probing astrophysical and dynamical processes in galactic centers.
AI.method: Statistical analysis of GWB from EMRIs, examining calculation methods, astrophysical source distribution, and key parameter influences (SMBH spin, CO masses).
AI.result: Eccentricity has negligible effect on GWB intensity due to rapid circularization. SMBH spin enhances characteristic strain by ~1%. BH-type COs produce ~10× stronger signals than NS or WD COs.
AI.conclusion: The GWB from EMRIs is significantly influenced by CO mass type, while eccentricity and SMBH spin have minor impacts.

title: Dark and Luminous Matter in the Coma Cluster: Probing Galaxy Cluster Assembly Through Filaments with Weak Lensing and Multiwavelength Observations
summary: The Coma cluster (Abell 1656; $z=0.023$) is a nearby rich galaxy cluster and a key laboratory for studying cluster assembly in the Cosmic Web. We characterize its projected dark matter distribution and connection to galaxies, the intracluster medium, and reported intracluster filaments (ICFs) with wide-field ($\sim$12-deg$^2$) Subaru/Hyper Suprime-Cam weak-lensing (WL) analysis. We reconstruct the two-dimensional mass distribution, fit Navarro-Frenk-White (NFW) models, derive an aperture mass densitometry profile, and compare the WL signal with optical spectroscopy, eROSITA X-ray observations, radio data, and gas fraction diagnostics. A single-halo NFW fit yields $M_{200\mathrm{c}}=8.2\pm0.7\times10^{14}~M_{\odot}$. The aperture mass profile agrees with the best-fit NFW model and the X-ray hydrostatic mass at $R\gtrsim20'$ ($\sim$560 kpc), suggesting little merger-induced bias in the global WL mass, while the inner region shows substantial hydrostatic bias. A two-halo NFW fit centered on NGC 4874 and NGC 4839 gives masses of $7.8\pm0.6$ and $0.9\pm0.2\times10^{14}~M_{\odot}$, implying a $\sim$1:8 minor merger. The gas mass fraction suggests that the system is returning from first apocenter. We find a positive spatial correlation between the WL signal and X-ray surface brightness, strongest along the ICF directions ($110^{\circ}$ and $340^{\circ}$), where shear-selected subhalos are predominantly detected. The Coma $r$-band mass-to-light ratio is radially constant with $\langle M/L_r\rangle\simeq250\pm66~M_{\odot}/L_{\odot}$ within $R_{200\mathrm{c}}$, whereas the northern and western ICFs show higher values of $\sim1000~M_{\odot}/L_{\odot}$, suggesting stronger dark matter dominance. These results show that joint WL and multiwavelength analyses can effectively probe cluster assembly and the dark matter content of ICFs.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a wide-field Subaru/Hyper Suprime-Cam weak-lensing analysis of the Coma cluster, characterizing its dark matter distribution, performing single and two-halo NFW fits, and comparing with multiwavelength data (X-ray, optical spectroscopy, radio) to study cluster assembly, merger dynamics, and intracluster filaments' dark matter content.
AI.motivation: The Coma cluster is a nearby rich galaxy cluster and a key laboratory for studying cluster assembly in the Cosmic Web. The goal is to characterize its projected dark matter distribution and connection to galaxies, the intracluster medium, and reported intracluster filaments (ICFs).
AI.method: Wide-field (~12 deg²) Subaru/Hyper Suprime-Cam weak-lensing analysis: two-dimensional mass reconstruction, NFW model fitting, aperture mass densitometry profile derivation, and comparison with optical spectroscopy, eROSITA X-ray observations, radio data, and gas fraction diagnostics.
AI.result: Single-halo NFW fit: M200c = 8.2 ± 0.7 × 10¹⁴ M☉. Two-halo fit yields masses of 7.8 ± 0.6 (NGC 4874) and 0.9 ± 0.2 × 10¹⁴ M☉ (NGC 4839), indicating a ~1:8 minor merger. Positive spatial correlation between WL signal and X-ray surface brightness, strongest along ICF directions. Radially constant M/Lr ~ 250 ± 66 M☉/L☉ within R200c, but ICFs show ~1000 M☉/L☉, suggesting stronger dark matter dominance.
AI.conclusion: Joint WL and multiwavelength analyses can effectively probe cluster assembly and the dark matter content of intracluster filaments. The gas mass fraction suggests the system is returning from first apocenter. Inner region shows substantial hydrostatic bias while outer region agrees with X-ray hydrostatic mass.

title: A Delayed Multi-channel Progenitor for Apparently Nonrepeating Fast Radio Bursts
summary: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are millisecond-duration radio flashes of unknown origin, observationally classified into repeating and apparently nonrepeating (one-off) populations. In this work, we use a statistical population approach to investigate the redshift evolution of one-off FRBs. We compare a pure star formation history (SFH) tracing model, phenomenological delayed models, physically motivated delayed models that correspond to binary neutron star related and neutron star age-window channels, and mixture models which is obtained when two physically motivated models are normalized separately and then combined as a weighted mixture. The samples in CHIME/FRB Catalog do not support an intrinsic event rate density that directly follows the SFH. The preferred model is mixture model corresponds to an effective mean delay time of $\barτ=1.426^{+0.032}_{-0.035}~\mathrm{Gyr}$. These results suggest that the current data may naturally explained by delayed, possibly multi-channel progenitor evolution for the one-off FRBs.

AI.tldr: This study uses statistical modeling on CHIME/FRB Catalog data to show that one-off FRBs do not directly trace star formation history but instead follow a delayed, multi-channel progenitor evolution model with an effective mean delay time of ~1.4 Gyr.
AI.motivation: To investigate the redshift evolution of one-off (apparently nonrepeating) FRBs and determine whether their intrinsic event rate density traces star formation history or involves delayed progenitor channels.
AI.method: Statistical population approach comparing multiple models: pure SFH-tracing model, phenomenological delayed models, physically motivated delayed models (binary neutron star related and neutron star age-window channels), and mixture models combining the two physically motivated models with weighted normalization.
AI.result: The CHIME/FRB Catalog data do not support an intrinsic event rate density that directly follows SFH. The preferred model is a mixture model with effective mean delay time $\barτ=1.426^{+0.032}_{-0.035}~\mathrm{Gyr}$.
AI.conclusion: Current data are naturally explained by delayed, possibly multi-channel progenitor evolution for one-off FRBs, rather than a simple SFH-tracing scenario.

title: Getting to know the Stellar Clusters in NGC 1569: Bayesian inference of stellar cluster properties in a dwarf starburst galaxy
summary: We present a Bayesian analysis of star clusters in the dwarf starburst galaxy NGC 1569 based on high-resolution Hubble Space Telescope imaging combined with integral-field spectroscopy from the Keck Cosmic Web Imager, obtained as part of the DUVET survey. For each cluster identified, we infer posterior probability distributions for mass and age using a forward modelling method that properly accounts for uncertainties due to stochastic sampling of the IMF. We investigate how the inferred properties depend on photometric coverage by repeating the analysis with different filter combinations, including mock extensions to the ultraviolet and near-infrared that emulate the addition of HST UV bands and James Webb Space Telescope imaging. We find that, while inclusion of these wavelength regimes further breaks age and mass degeneracies, the currently available data yields reasonably strong constraints on cluster parameters. We compare inferred cluster properties to the conditions of the local interstellar medium, and find evidence for multiple interesting correlations. The truncation mass of the cluster mass function varies with galactocentric distance, particularly moving off the disk, consistent with a dependence on the density of the interstellar medium. Cluster mass positively correlates with metallicity, suggesting that massive clusters preferentially form in pre-enriched gas, and the ionisation state of the gas, reflecting the increased prevalence of high-mass stars in high-mass clusters. These results demonstrate the power of Bayesian, initial mass function-aware modelling for resolving cluster populations in nearby starburst dwarfs and provide new insight into how cluster formation and feedback respond to local galactic conditions.

AI.tldr: Bayesian analysis of star clusters in NGC 1569 using HST and KCWI/DUVET data, with forward modeling accounting for stochastic IMF sampling, reveals that cluster mass function truncation varies with galactocentric distance, cluster mass correlates with metallicity, and ionization state depends on cluster mass.
AI.motivation: To understand how star cluster formation and feedback respond to local galactic conditions in dwarf starburst galaxies, and to demonstrate the power of Bayesian, IMF-aware modeling for resolving cluster populations.
AI.method: Forward modeling with Bayesian inference to derive posterior probability distributions for cluster mass and age, accounting for stochastic IMF sampling. Analysis repeated with different filter combinations (including mock UV and NIR extensions) to assess parameter constraints.
AI.result: Current data provides reasonably strong constraints on cluster parameters; UV/NIR photometry further breaks age-mass degeneracies. Cluster mass function truncation depends on galactocentric distance (correlated with ISM density). Cluster mass positively correlates with metallicity and gas ionization state.
AI.conclusion: Bayesian, IMF-aware modeling is powerful for resolving cluster populations in nearby starburst dwarfs. Cluster properties are linked to local ISM conditions, with massive clusters preferentially forming in pre-enriched, dense environments.

title: Deep optical spectroscopic monitoring of the pulsating ULX NGC 1313 X-2 with longslit Gemini observations
summary: This study reports the nature of the companion star to the pulsating ULX NGC 1313 X-2, using long-slit spectroscopic data from Gemini-South observations, based on archival data from 2009. After stacking flux-calibrated spectra from ten nights of observations and fitting the spectra with stellar templates, we find a possible Balmer break in the GMOS-S spectrum below 4000 Angstroms, which is suggestive of an A-type supergiant donor. Using the inferred stellar radii, we report updated constraints on the orbital parameters of the system and on the nature of the binary. We also add some information on the accretion disc size scale by studying the X-ray and optical variability using the lag-frequency spectrum and corroborate on results from earlier studies for the gas bubble expansion rates by modelling the [O III] emission line profiles, allowing constraints on the kinetic power of the wind/jet relative to the accretion power. This study also expands on previous efforts to study the formation history of the binary using multi-wavelength observations.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes the companion star of the pulsating ULX NGC 1313 X-2 using Gemini-South spectroscopic data, identifying a possible A-type supergiant donor via Balmer break detection, and provides updated orbital constraints, accretion disc size estimates from X-ray/optical variability, and wind/jet kinetic power constraints from [O III] line modeling.
AI.motivation: To characterize the nature of the companion star in the pulsating ultraluminous X-ray source NGC 1313 X-2 and constrain the binary system's orbital parameters, accretion disc properties, and formation history.
AI.method: Stacked flux-calibrated spectra (Gemini-South/GMOS-S, archival 2009 data) fitted with stellar templates; X-ray and optical variability analysis via lag-frequency spectrum; [O III] emission line profile modeling for gas bubble expansion.
AI.result: Detection of a possible Balmer break below 4000 Å suggestive of an A-type supergiant donor; updated orbital parameter constraints; accretion disc size constraints from variability; wind/jet kinetic power estimates relative to accretion power.
AI.conclusion: The companion is likely an A-type supergiant; multi-wavelength analysis yields refined binary parameters and accretion-wind energetics.

title: DESI as sparse Integral Field Spectrograph I: Spatially resolved chemical enrichment in star-forming galaxies at $z\leq0.1$
comment: Submitted to The Astrophysical Journal; comments are welcome
summary: We present a spatially resolved chemical abundance analysis of 2291 star-forming galaxies at $z \leq 0.1$, spanning nearly four orders of magnitude in stellar mass ($8 \le \rm log (M_{\star}/M_{\odot}) \le 11.5$), by exploiting the multi-fibre spectra from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) as a sparse integral field spectrograph. In the inner regions ($<2R_e$), the radial gas-phase metallicity profiles show an outward-declining trend for massive galaxies, with the steepest gradient ($\nabla_{log(O/H)}$) $\sim-0.08$ dex/R$_{e}$, whereas low-mass dwarf galaxies exhibit nearly flat profiles ($\nabla_{log(O/H)}\sim-0.02$ dex/R$_{e}$). The large galactocentric radii ($\sim$5 R$_{e}$) probed in this study, reveal flat metallicity profiles near the disk-halo interface. Strikingly, these flat metallicity values are consistent across a wide stellar mass range, likely reflecting the influence of low SFR and metal poor inflows in the outer regions. The metallicity gradient - stellar mass relation exhibits a turnover at $\log(M_\star/M_\odot) \sim 10.5$, beyond which gradients become shallower, possibly driven by the chemical equilibrium in the inner disk of massive galaxies and/or dilution from cosmic gas accretion. At fixed stellar mass, a strong size dependence is observed, where compact galaxies show flatter gradients and higher central enrichment than their extended counterparts. The abundance gradients are further linked with the stellar age distribution within the galactic disk, where galaxies with younger outskirts show steeper gradients than the ones with older outskirts, consistent with ongoing inside-out disc growth sustaining centrally concentrated chemical enrichment. These results underscore the interplay of star formation efficiency, stellar feedback, and metal-poor gas accretion in governing the radial chemical structure in galaxies.

AI.tldr: This study uses DESI multi-fibre spectra to analyze spatially resolved chemical abundances of 2,291 star-forming galaxies at z ≤ 0.1, finding that massive galaxies have steep outward-declining metallicity gradients while low-mass dwarfs show flat profiles, with gradients flattening at large radii (~5 Re). The metallicity gradient–stellar mass relation turns over at log(M*/M⊙) ~ 10.5, and compact galaxies display flatter gradients and higher central enrichment than extended ones at fixed mass.
AI.motivation: To understand how radial chemical abundance patterns in galaxies are shaped by processes such as star formation efficiency, feedback, and gas accretion, across a wide range of stellar masses and sizes.
AI.method: Spatially resolved chemical abundance analysis of 2,291 star-forming galaxies at z ≤ 0.1 using DESI multi-fibre spectra as a sparse integral field spectrograph, probing galactocentric radii up to ~5 Re.
AI.result: Massive galaxies show steep metallicity gradients (~−0.08 dex/Re) while low-mass dwarfs are nearly flat (~−0.02 dex/Re); profiles become flat at large radii (~5 Re) with consistent values across mass. Gradient–mass relation turns over at log(M*/M⊙) ~ 10.5; compact galaxies have flatter gradients and higher central enrichment; younger outskirts correlate with steeper gradients.
AI.conclusion: The radial chemical structure in galaxies results from the interplay of star formation efficiency, stellar feedback, and metal-poor gas accretion; inside-out disk growth drives centrally concentrated enrichment.

title: Multi-Epoch X-Ray Detection of SLSN-I 2018bsz: Constraints on the Powering Mechanism and Ejecta Structure
comment: 18 Pages, 5 Figures, 3 Tables. Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: SN 2018bsz is the closest known stripped superluminous supernova (SLSN-I) to date, making it an ideal laboratory for investigating the physical mechanisms powering this class of extreme explosions. We present a multi-epoch X-ray spectroscopic study of SN 2018bsz based on four Chandra observations followed by one XMM observation, spanning 87 to 1253 days after explosion. The source is detected at all Chandra epochs and is also tentatively detected in the late XMM observation, although more uncertain due to nearby contaminating sources. Regardless of the XMM detection, this makes SN 2018bsz the second X-ray detected SLSN-I and the third X-ray detected SLSN overall. We explore potential power sources for the observed X-ray emission and find that a millisecond (ms) magnetar central engine underpredict most of the observed X-ray luminosities and fail to reproduce the relatively flat light curve. Accounting for ejecta absorption further increases the discrepancy. While asymmetries and magnetar-driven ionization could reduce the effective absorption, ionization breakout is expected years after our observational window. Instead, the observations are more readily explained by early-time interaction between the ejecta and the circumstellar medium, while the magnetar emission is absorbed by the ejecta. This scenario is supported by the flat temporal evolution, previous optical results, and inferred mass-loss rates which resemble those of stripped SNe that later evolve into interacting systems. Our results thus favor the scenario where SN 2018bsz is part of a distinct group of SLSN-I, where interaction is crucial for the strong emission.

AI.tldr: SN 2018bsz, the closest stripped superluminous supernova (SLSN-I), was studied in X-rays from 87 to 1253 days post-explosion. It is the second X-ray detected SLSN-I and third SLSN overall. The observed flat X-ray light curve disfavors a millisecond magnetar central engine (even with ejecta absorption) and is better explained by ejecta-circumstellar medium interaction, suggesting SN 2018bsz belongs to a subgroup of SLSN-I where interaction powers the strong emission.
AI.motivation: To investigate the physical mechanisms powering stripped superluminous supernovae (SLSN-I) by studying the closest known example, SN 2018bsz, through multi-epoch X-ray observations, testing the magnetar central engine model versus ejecta-CSM interaction.
AI.method: Multi-epoch X-ray spectroscopic study using four Chandra observations and one XMM-Newton observation spanning 87–1253 days after explosion; modeling of X-ray light curves and comparison with predictions from magnetar and interaction models.
AI.result: SN 2018bsz is the second X-ray detected SLSN-I and third SLSN overall. The magnetar model underpredicts observed X-ray luminosities and fails to reproduce the flat light curve; accounting for ejecta absorption worsens the discrepancy. The flat temporal evolution and inferred mass-loss rates favor ejecta-CSM interaction as the power source.
AI.conclusion: The observed X-ray emission from SN 2018bsz is better explained by early-time ejecta-CSM interaction rather than a magnetar central engine, placing SN 2018bsz in a distinct subgroup of SLSN-I where interaction is crucial for the strong emission.

title: Constraining the Geometry of Galactic Dark Matter with Gaia Data Release 3
comment: 21 pages, 8 figures, accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: We derive both the mid-plane and off-plane rotation curves, $v_c(R,z)$, and the vertical acceleration, $a_z(R,z)$, of the Milky Way (MW) using \textit{Gaia}~DR3 data over the ranges of vertical heights $z \in (-2,2)\,$ kpc and galactocentric distances $R \in (8.5,14)$ kpc where the velocity components are determined with high precision, i.e., with an error $< 5\%$. In contrast, the vertical acceleration $a_z(R,z)$ is dominated by model-dependent systematics, with uncertainties of up to $\sim 20\%$. This level of accuracy allows us to place stringent constraints on the geometry of the MW's dark matter (DM) distribution, as the vertical gradients of the gravitational potential attain their maximum within this range of radial and vertical distances corresponding to the characteristic scales of the disk. We find that models including the observed stellar components together with a spherical DM halo fail to reproduce both the pronounced variation of $v_c(R,z)$ with height and the observed behavior of $a_z(R,z)$. In particular, spherical halos with a scale radius of $r_s \sim 15$ kpc contribute negligibly to the off-plane rotation curve and vertical acceleration in the inner disk, leaving these features primarily determined by the stellar mass distribution. Conversely, models in which DM is confined to a flattened, disk-like configuration predict substantial contributions to both $v_c(R,z)$ and $a_z(R,z)$, resulting in a markedly better agreement with the data. We conclude that disk-like DM distributions are strongly favored over spherical halo models. Forthcoming Gaia data releases will enable even more stringent tests of the geometry and distribution of the MW's DM component.

AI.tldr: Using Gaia DR3 data, this paper derives rotation curves and vertical accelerations of the Milky Way (within R=8.5-14 kpc, |z|<2 kpc) and shows that spherical dark matter halo models fail to reproduce the observed height-dependent variations, whereas flattened, disk-like dark matter distributions provide substantially better agreement, strongly favoring a disk-like geometry for the MW's dark matter.
AI.motivation: To constrain the geometry (spherical vs. flattened/disk-like) of the Milky Way's dark matter distribution using high-precision Gaia DR3 kinematic data, particularly vertical gradients of the gravitational potential where sensitivity to DM is maximal.
AI.method: Derived mid-plane and off-plane rotation curves v_c(R,z) and vertical acceleration a_z(R,z) from Gaia DR3 over R∈(8.5,14) kpc and z∈(-2,2) kpc, selecting data with velocity error <5%. Compared these measurements to models with spherical DM halos (scale radius ~15 kpc) plus stellar components vs. models with flattened, disk-like DM distributions.
AI.result: Spherical DM halos fail to reproduce the observed height variation of v_c(R,z) and a_z(R,z), contributing negligibly to off-plane rotation and vertical acceleration in the inner disk. Disk-like DM models show substantial contributions to both v_c and a_z, yielding markedly better agreement with data.
AI.conclusion: Disk-like (flattened) dark matter distributions are strongly favored over spherical halo models for the Milky Way. Future Gaia data releases will enable even more stringent tests of DM geometry.

title: Classification of Compact Stars via Machine Learning and Neural Network Models
comment: 22 pages, 12 figures, 15 tables. Any comments are welcome
summary: Recent advances in multimessenger astronomy, particularly through gravitational-wave observations of compact-object mergers, have significantly improved our understanding of dense matter. Nevertheless, the internal composition of compact stars remains uncertain. Depending on the underlying equation of state (EoS), these objects may be neutron stars composed primarily of nucleons, quark stars made of deconfined quark matter, or hybrid stars containing both hadronic and quark phases. More exotic constituents, such as hyperons, meson condensates, or dark matter, have also been proposed. In this work, we investigate whether the internal composition of compact stars can be inferred from observable quantities, including mass, radius, and tidal deformability. To address this problem, we employ machine-learning and deep-learning techniques trained on a larg dataset of EoSs describing both neutron stars and quark stars. From these EoSs, we generate the corresponding mass radius relations spanning a wide range of stellar configurations. The resulting dataset is used to train and evaluate classification models aimed at identifying the nature of compact objects from their macroscopic properties. Our results indicate that suitable combinations of observables can distinguish neutron stars from quark stars with very high accuracy. These findings demonstrate the potential of machine-learning approaches as tools for probing the composition of dense matter. However, further studies incorporating additional scenarios, including hybrid stars and other exotic forms of matter, are required to establish the robustness and general applicability of this methodology.

AI.tldr: This paper uses machine learning and deep learning on a large dataset of equations of state to classify compact stars (neutron stars vs. quark stars) based on observable properties (mass, radius, tidal deformability), achieving high accuracy, but notes further work is needed for hybrid and exotic matter scenarios.
AI.motivation: The internal composition of compact stars (neutron stars, quark stars, hybrid stars, or exotic matter) remains uncertain. The authors aim to determine whether composition can be inferred from observable quantities like mass, radius, and tidal deformability.
AI.method: Machine-learning and deep-learning classification models were trained on a large dataset of equation of state (EoS) descriptions for both neutron stars and quark stars. Corresponding mass-radius relations were generated across a wide range of stellar configurations, and the dataset was used to train/evaluate classification models.
AI.result: Suitable combinations of observables can distinguish neutron stars from quark stars with very high accuracy using the trained models.
AI.conclusion: Machine-learning approaches demonstrate potential as tools for probing dense matter composition, but further studies incorporating hybrid stars and other exotic matter forms are needed for robustness and general applicability.

title: CAPOS: The bulge Cluster APOgee Survey XII. Abundances for 98 PIGS metal-poor Bulge field giants
summary: The inner Milky Way hosts overlapping stellar populations (bar--bulge, inner thin and thick disks, and halo), complicating population assignments along the line of sight. A joint chemical--dynamical approach is required to isolate a clean field bulge sample. Metal-poor bulge stars are valuable as they likely trace the earliest phases of chemical enrichment in the inner Galaxy. We aim to characterize the alpha-element (Si, Mg) and selected Fe-peak abundances of a dynamically defined sample of bulge field stars, and to contrast these trends with the inner-halo tail in the metal-poor regime. We analyze metal-poor candidates from the Pristine Inner Galaxy Survey observed by the bulge Cluster APOGEE Survey. Using APOGEE/ASPCAP abundances (S/N >= 50), we integrate full 6D orbits in a barred Milky Way potential. Bulge membership is defined via orbital confinement using an apocenter cut and the high-density locus in the (E_J, L_z) plane, with uncertainties estimated using Monte Carlo simulations. We identify 98 stars as bulge members. The metallicity distribution spans -2.5 <= [Fe/H] <= -0.4, with a median [Fe/H] = -1.71, offset to higher metallicity than the inner halo (median [Fe/H] = -1.96). The sample follows a high-alpha sequence with slopes d[Si/Fe]/d[Fe/H] = -0.020(+0.012,-0.051) and d[Mg/Fe]/d[Fe/H] = -0.097(+0.062,-0.133). Fe-peak tracers show [Ni/Fe] ~ 0, while [Mn/Fe] declines with [Fe/H] with a mild upturn at higher metallicity. We detect no significant [Si/Fe] gradients with R_apo or Z_max (+0.010(+0.018,0.000) and +0.006(+0.022,-0.011) dex kpc^-1, respectively). Results are insensitive to Omega_p, yielding indistinguishable memberships. The chemo-orbital evidence favors an in situ origin within the inner Galaxy for the metal-poor bulge field, enriched at early times and rearranged by secular bar evolution, with a minor contribution from halo stars at the most metal-poor end.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes 98 dynamically defined metal-poor bulge field stars from the inner Milky Way using APOGEE/ASPCAP abundances and 6D orbital integration. The sample shows high-alpha sequences, no significant radial gradients, and chemo-orbital evidence supporting an in situ origin within the inner Galaxy, enriched early and rearranged by secular bar evolution, with minor halo contamination at the most metal-poor end.
AI.motivation: The inner Milky Way contains multiple overlapping stellar populations (bar-bulge, thin/thick disks, halo), making population assignments difficult. Metal-poor bulge stars are valuable tracers of early chemical enrichment in the inner Galaxy, but require a joint chemical-dynamical approach to isolate a clean field bulge sample.
AI.method: Metal-poor candidates from the Pristine Inner Galaxy Survey were observed by the bulge Cluster APOGEE Survey. APOGEE/ASPCAP abundances (S/N >= 50) were used, and full 6D orbits were integrated in a barred Milky Way potential. Bulge membership was defined via orbital confinement using an apocenter cut and the high-density locus in the (E_J, L_z) plane, with Monte Carlo uncertainty estimation.
AI.result: 98 bulge members identified with [Fe/H] range -2.5 to -0.4 (median -1.71). Sample follows high-alpha sequences with slopes d[Si/Fe]/d[Fe/H] = -0.020 and d[Mg/Fe]/d[Fe/H] = -0.097. [Ni/Fe] ~ 0, [Mn/Fe] declines with [Fe/H] with mild upturn. No significant [Si/Fe] gradients with R_apo or Z_max. Results insensitive to Omega_p.
AI.conclusion: Chemo-orbital evidence favors an in situ origin within the inner Galaxy for the metal-poor bulge field, enriched at early times and rearranged by secular bar evolution, with a minor contribution from halo stars at the most metal-poor end.

title: Simulations of 3-Dimensional Recoil Response to Coherent Elastic Neutrino-Nucleus Scattering Events in Directional Direct Dark Matter Detectors
summary: Following our earlier work on studying 3-dimensional nuclear recoil response to Galactic Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs) in directional direct Dark Matter detectors, in this paper, we simulate 3-D coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering (CEvNS) events induced by Solar B-8 neutrinos. Our numerical results show that, in contrast to the approximately fixed patterns of the WIMP-induced signals, the characteristic ring-like angular distributions of the nuclear recoil flux/energy of CEvNS events show clearly annual variations along the trajectories of the moving direction of incident Solar neutrinos in different celestial coordinate systems without experimentally distinguishable target dependence.

AI.tldr: This paper simulates 3-D CEvNS events from Solar B-8 neutrinos, showing that unlike fixed WIMP patterns, CEvNS produces ring-like angular distributions with annual variations dependent on Solar neutrino direction, independent of target material.
AI.motivation: To extend prior work on WIMP-induced nuclear recoil responses to study CEvNS events from Solar B-8 neutrinos, and to characterize their distinctive signatures compared to WIMP signals for directional Dark Matter detectors.
AI.method: 3-D simulation of coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering (CEvNS) events induced by Solar B-8 neutrinos, analyzing nuclear recoil flux/energy angular distributions.
AI.result: CEvNS events show characteristic ring-like angular distributions with clear annual variations along Solar neutrino trajectories in different celestial coordinate systems, unlike the fixed patterns of WIMP signals. No experimentally distinguishable target dependence was found.
AI.conclusion: The distinct annual-varying ring-like patterns of CEvNS can be used to differentiate Solar neutrino backgrounds from WIMP signals in directional Dark Matter detectors.

title: Influence of the resonance ring gravity on the stellar velocity distribution near the OLR of the Galactic bar
comment: 14 pages, 5 figures, accepted for publication in Astrophysical Bulletin
summary: We constructed the 2D model of the Galaxy which initially includes an analytical bar, bulge, disk and halo. The model disk forms the outer elliptical resonance rings R1 and R2 located near the outer Lindblad resonance of the bar (OLR), as well as the inner resonance ring r located near the corotation radius (CR). As the density of stars in the elliptical rings increased, we introduced additional gravitational perturbations created by the rings. The radial component of gravitational perturbations from the elliptical rings, F_R, at a point with the Galactocentric coordinates (R, theta) was represented as a combination of three polynomials in powers R/Re or Re/R, where Re is the distance to the midline (middle) of the ring at a given angle theta. The azimuthal component of the disturbances, F_T, was calculated using the force F_R. The difference between the values of the force F_R (F_T) calculated using the numerical differentiation of the potential and using the analytical representation does not exceed 5.7% (1.3%) of the maximum value of the force F_R generated by the elliptical rings. In general, the gravity of the elliptical rings has little effect on the process of adjustment of epicyclic motions near the OLR of the bar.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a 2D Galactic model with a bar, bulge, disk, and halo, focusing on elliptical resonance rings (R1, R2 near OLR, and r near CR). The authors introduce gravitational perturbations from these rings, representing the radial force component as polynomials of R/Re or Re/R, and derive the azimuthal component from it. The analytical force approximation deviates <5.7% (radial) and <1.3% (azimuthal) from numerical differentiation. The ring gravity has minimal effect on epicyclic motion adjustment near the bar's OLR.
AI.motivation: To construct a realistic 2D Galactic model that includes elliptical resonance rings and analytically represent their gravitational perturbations to study their impact on stellar dynamics near resonance regions.
AI.method: A 2D Galaxy model with analytical bar, bulge, disk, and halo is built. Elliptical resonance rings (R1, R2 at OLR; r at CR) form in the disk. Their gravitational perturbations are represented using polynomials in powers of R/Re or Re/R for the radial component (F_R), with the azimuthal component (F_T) derived from F_R.
AI.result: The analytical force representation achieves high accuracy: radial force error ≤5.7% and azimuthal force error ≤1.3% relative to the maximum radial force from the rings. The gravitational influence of the elliptical rings on epicyclic motion adjustment near the OLR is minor.
AI.conclusion: The proposed analytical representation of elliptical ring gravity is accurate and efficient. However, the rings do not significantly affect the dynamics of epicyclic motions near the bar's outer Lindblad resonance.

title: Feedback-Free Star Formation in Clusters within a Galaxy Simulated at High Resolution in Cosmic Dawn
comment: 15 pages, 17 figures. Submitted to MNRAS. All comments are welcome
summary: We perform a cosmological zoom-in simulation of a massive galaxy ($M_s\sim10^{10}\rm M_\odot$ at $z\sim10$) using the GIZMO code. By employing $\leq 3\rm pc$ resolution and a $3.4\rm Myr$ supernova feedback delay, we capture the feedback-free starbursts (FFB) in clusters. The simulation reproduces FFB model predictions and super-bright galaxies observed by JWST. At $z\sim10$, cold streams feed a compact galaxy ($R_{\rm e}\sim1\rm kpc$), with stellar and surface densities ($>10^5\rm cm^{-3}$, $>10^5\rm M_\odot pc^{-2}$) exceeding FFB thresholds. The global star-formation efficiency (SFE) is $\varepsilon_s\sim0.2\text{--}0.3$, associated with a fluctuating star-formation history. We identified over $10^5$ star clusters ($M_{\star}>10^{4.5}\rm M_\odot$) with a nearly scale-free mass distribution (${\rm d}N/{{\rm d}\log M}\propto M^{-1.06}$). Approximately 90\% of star formation occurs in clusters, which at a given time constitute $30\text{--}40\%$ of the total stellar mass. The star formation in most of the clusters of masses $<10^7\rm M_\odot$, occurs in bursts of $<3\rm Myr$ and a local SFE $\sim0.5\pm 0.2$. Cluster metallicities ($-2.01<\log (Z/Z_\odot)<-0.45$) indicate rapid baryon recycling. Feedback-driven outflows exhibit typical temperature of $10^7\rm K$ and typical velocities of $\sim 2000\rm km\ s^{-1}$. In the highly dynamic central $1\rm kpc$, clusters undergo rapid orbital decay and merge to assemble the oblate nuclear stellar cluster. Cluster shapes range from oblate to prolate, with a triaxial median. These clusters are consistent with JWST observations, and a fraction of them may survive to yield the globular clusters (GCs) at low redshifts.

AI.tldr: A cosmological zoom-in simulation of a massive z~10 galaxy reveals feedback-free starbursts in clusters, reproducing JWST observations of super-bright galaxies. It finds ~90% of star formation occurs in ~10^5 star clusters with scale-free mass distribution, rapid baryon recycling, and cluster properties consistent with potential globular cluster progenitors.
AI.motivation: To understand the formation of super-bright galaxies observed by JWST at high redshift and test the feedback-free starburst (FFB) model predictions through direct numerical simulation at sufficient resolution.
AI.method: Cosmological zoom-in simulation using GIZMO code with ≤3 pc resolution, 3.4 Myr supernova feedback delay, tracking star cluster formation and dynamics in a massive galaxy at z~10.
AI.result: Found 10^5+ star clusters with scale-free mass distribution (dN/dlogM ∝ M^-1.06), ~90% of star formation in clusters, SFE ε_s~0.2-0.3, cluster burst timescales <3 Myr, local SFE ~0.5±0.2, metallicities -2.01<log(Z/Z⊙)<-0.45, feedback-driven outflows at ~10^7 K and ~2000 km/s.
AI.conclusion: The simulation successfully reproduces FFB model predictions and JWST observations; the formed star clusters are consistent with being progenitors of globular clusters observed at low redshifts.

title: Carbon Abundances in Metal-Poor Stars Reveal Distinct Galaxy and Star Formation Pathways in the Early Universe
summary: Carbon-enhanced metal-poor (CEMP; with $\rm{[Fe/H]} \le -2.0$ and $\rm{[C/Fe]} \ge 0.7$) stars preserve information about early chemical enrichment, low-mass star formation, and the hierarchical assembly of galaxies. In this study, we have compiled an extensive literature sample of 1032 stellar carbon abundances spanning the metal-poor Milky Way halo (437 stars), 21 ultra-faint dwarf galaxies (UFDs; 102 stars), seven classical dwarf spheroidal galaxies (254 stars), three accreted dwarf galaxies (90 stars), the Small Accreted Stellar Systems (SASS; 77 stars), and eleven stellar streams (72 stars). We establish the fractions of CEMP stars for each of these systems and categories. Generally, the low-mass UFDs possess the high fractions at low metallicities, whereas the more massive classical dwarf galaxies have relatively few CEMP stars. This behavior reveals a new low-metallicity Magnitude ($M_{\rm V}$)--CEMP Fraction relation across the dwarf satellite galaxy population. The high CEMP fractions in surviving UFDs suggest their enrichment was dominated by faint supernovae, as higher energy input would likely have quenched star production. The low CEMP fractions in classical dwarfs imply predominantly in situ formation rather than assembly from smaller systems. Using $\rm{[C/H]}$ abundances, we also probe early low-mass star formation. Eight stars lie within or near the theoretical ''forbidden zone'', indicating that dust-induced cooling, alongside fine-structure line cooling, contributed to early star formation. These rare dust-cooled stars may have formed in UFD-like systems that did not survive. Overall, the metal-poor Milky Way halo appears to have assembled from many different dwarf galaxies, with CEMP halo stars being contributed by early UFD-like systems and non-CEMP halo stars by intermediate-sized halos that later formed classical dwarfs.

AI.tldr: This paper compiles 1032 carbon abundances across Milky Way halo, dwarf galaxies, and stellar streams to establish CEMP star fractions, revealing a magnitude-CEMP fraction relation where ultra-faint dwarfs have high CEMP fractions (from faint supernova enrichment) while classical dwarfs have low fractions (suggesting in-situ formation). Eight stars in the "forbidden zone" indicate dust-induced cooling contributed to early low-mass star formation. The Milky Way halo assembled from diverse dwarf galaxies.
AI.motivation: To understand early chemical enrichment, low-mass star formation, and hierarchical assembly of galaxies by analyzing carbon-enhanced metal-poor (CEMP) stars across different stellar systems and environments.
AI.method: Compiled a literature sample of 1032 stellar carbon abundances from 437 Milky Way halo stars, 102 stars from 21 UFDs, 254 stars from 7 classical dSph galaxies, 90 stars from 3 accreted dwarfs, 77 SASS stars, and 72 stars from 11 stellar streams, then computed CEMP fractions for each system.
AI.result: Found a low-metallicity MV–CEMP fraction relation across dwarf satellites: low-mass UFDs have high CEMP fractions, classical dwarfs have few CEMP stars. Eight stars lie near the theoretical "forbidden zone" for low-mass star formation, suggesting dust-induced cooling contributed to early star formation.
AI.conclusion: The Milky Way halo assembled from many dwarf galaxies: CEMP halo stars came from early UFD-like systems enriched by faint supernovae, while non-CEMP halo stars came from intermediate-sized halos that later formed classical dwarfs. Classical dwarfs formed predominantly in situ rather than from assembly of smaller systems.

title: The X-ray photon index Eddington ratio relation in radio-quiet quasars from XMM-Newton and SDSS
summary: This study presents a comprehensive X-ray spectroscopic analysis of 642 quasars, obtained by cross-matching the XMM-Newton Serendipitous Source Catalog (DR11) with the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (DR16) quasar catalog. After stringent quality filtering and automated spectral reduction, we derived reliable photon indices ($Γ$) and intrinsic 2--10 keV X-ray luminosities. Using multiwavelength data, sources were classified into 561 radio-quiet (RQ) and 81 radio-loud (RL) quasars. We estimate the bolometric luminosity and Eddington ratio ($λ_{\mathrm{Edd}}$) from absorption-corrected X-ray measurements and virial black hole masses. Our primary objective is to establish and characterize the fundamental relationship between the photon index and Eddington ratio for RQ population. We find that RQ quasars exhibit systematically higher Eddington ratios, peaking at $\log λ_{\mathrm{Edd}} \approx -1.2$, and softer spectra with $Γ\approx 2.0$. A statistically significant positive correlation between $Γ$ and $λ_{\mathrm{Edd}}$ is detected in RQ quasars, supporting disk--corona coupling models. To validate our results within the broader context of AGN evolution, we further examine the dependence of $λ_{\mathrm{Edd}}$ on redshift ($z$) and black hole mass ($M_{\mathrm{BH}}$). For RQ quasars, $λ_{\mathrm{Edd}}$ increases with redshift and decreases with $M_{\mathrm{BH}}$, in strong agreement with recent results \cite{aggarwal2024evidence}, highlighting the universal nature of these accretion trends. By correlating spectral slope with accretion rate, this work provides new insights into the interplay between accretion physics, jet activity, and the cosmic evolution of quasars.
